name: Old Bend
label: Old Bend
about_prose: Old Bend is where the city started. It is bounded by the Deschutes River to the west, Drake Park and Franklin Avenue to the north, Highway 97 to the east, and Arizona Avenue to the south, roughly 1 square mile, and it is the smallest of the city's neighborhood association districts. Alexander M. Drake subdivided the land in 1910 through the Pilot Butte Development Company, selling the original lots for $100 to $250. The Oregon Trunk Railroad reached Bend in 1911, and the Shevlin-Hixon and Brooks-Scanlon mills opened within a month of each other in 1916, Shevlin-Hixon in March and Brooks-Scanlon in April. Bend's population went from 536 people in 1910 to 5,414 by 1920, and most of Old Bend's housing stock was built to hold that growth: small lots, alley-loaded garages, homes sized for millworkers rather than for show.

That history is why the neighborhood looks the way it does. The Drake Park Neighborhood Historic District, listed on the National Register of Historic Places on June 3, 2005 (NRHP reference 05000380), covers 17 city blocks and 83 residential lots inside Old Bend, with 82 percent of the homes built between 1910 and 1954. Fourteen architectural styles show up across those lots, led by 25 Craftsman bungalows and 17 homes in the various Colonial styles, with English Cottage, Tudor, Dutch Colonial, Spanish Colonial Revival, Georgian Revival, and California Ranch in smaller numbers. Four houses were individually listed on the National Register before the district designation: the Putnam House at 606 NW Congress (1911), the McCann House at 440 NW Congress (1915), the Moore House (1921), and the Hamilton House (1923).

The district designation is not just a plaque. Nearly any visible exterior change inside the historic boundary, paint color, window replacement, roofing, an addition, a fence, requires review under the city's historic preservation code, and that applies to contributing structures whether or not they carry an individual landmark listing. Buying a house here usually means buying into that process for any exterior work, which is slower and more constrained than remodeling a house outside the district.

Old Bend was not always the neighborhood it is today. The Old Bend Neighborhood Association, founded in the early 2000s, has described the area in the 1980s, after the local timber industry contracted, as a place where residents burned garbage in wood stoves, cars sat on blocks in front of houses, and yards went to weed. The turnaround since then has been steady rather than sudden. The housing stock did not change. What changed was who wanted to live a walk from downtown.

Drake Park sits at the neighborhood's north edge, established by the city in 1921 on 13 acres with close to half a mile of Deschutes River frontage, bought for $21,000 after the Women's Civic League collected 1,500 signatures to keep the land from being subdivided. The Deschutes River Trail runs through the park, connecting Old Bend on foot or by bike to downtown, which sits inside the neighborhood's eastern edge along Wall and Bond Streets. William E. Miller Elementary, a Bend-La Pine Schools K-5 built to LEED Gold standards at 300 NW Crosby Drive, serves the area.

The trade-off of that location is parking, and it is not a minor one. Old Bend sits wedged between downtown, the river, and Drake Park, and for years the neighborhood's residential streets absorbed the overflow: downtown shoppers, restaurant and bar employees, river floaters headed to the put-in, and Drake Park visitors all competing for the same curb space as residents. The city ran the Old Bend Parking District as a pilot starting in December 2020 and made it permanent in December 2021. Residents and their guests now need a permit to use most of the neighborhood's roughly 570 residential parking spaces. Visitors are limited to a smaller set of two-hour and four-hour spaces, with citations enforced. The program exists because, without it, living a few blocks from downtown meant not being able to park in front of your own house on a summer weekend.

There is no homeowners association here, no shared amenities to fund, and no architectural committee beyond the city's historic review. What you get instead is a house inside the city's original townsite, within walking distance of Wall and Bond Streets and Drake Park, on a lot laid out in 1910. What comes with it is a set of exterior-remodel rules tied to the historic district and a parking permit system tied to the location. It suits someone who wants the historic core and downtown on foot, and is willing to trade yard size and easy street parking for it.

amenities.name: Drake Park and Mirror Pond
amenities.description: A 13-acre park established in 1921 at 777 NW Riverside Blvd, with nearly half a mile of Deschutes River frontage, open lawns, an outdoor stage, and the Deschutes River Trail.

amenities.name: Drake Park Neighborhood Historic District
amenities.description: Listed on the National Register June 3, 2005 (NRHP 05000380), covering 17 blocks and 83 homes in 14 architectural styles built mainly 1910 to the 1930s.

amenities.name: Deschutes River Trail
amenities.description: A paved multi-use path through Drake Park along the river, connecting Old Bend to downtown and the wider Bend trail network.

amenities.name: William E. Miller Elementary
amenities.description: A Bend-La Pine Schools K-5 at 300 NW Crosby Dr serving the Old Bend area, in a LEED Gold building.

amenities.name: Downtown Bend
amenities.description: The Wall Street and Bond Street commercial core sits within and beside Old Bend, putting grocery, retail, and dining within a 5-to-10-minute walk of most addresses.
